title: World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson
lead: A New York family drives its Audi through Oklahoma and suffers a catastrophic fire. The injured family sues the distribution chain, but the regional distributor and local dealer challenge the state’s authority over them.

actors.name: Harry and Kay Eloise Robinson and their children
actors.role: New York purchasers traveling to a new Arizona home; Kay and two children suffered burns.

actors.name: Seaway Volkswagen, Inc.
actors.role: New York retail dealer that sold the Audi.

actors.name: World-Wide Volkswagen Corporation
actors.role: New York regional distributor serving New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.

actors.name: Audi and Volkswagen of America
actors.role: Manufacturer and importer; remained defendants outside this Supreme Court proceeding.

actors.name: Charles S. Woodson
actors.role: Creek County judge named as respondent in the requested writ of prohibition.

proceedings: The Creek County trial court rejected the distributor’s and dealer’s special jurisdictional objections and denied reconsideration.
On October 10, 1978, the Oklahoma Supreme Court assumed original jurisdiction but denied prohibition.
The U.S. Supreme Court reversed six to three on January 21, 1980; the manufacturer and importer remained defendants below.
limits: This account follows the canonical historical brief, without a new opinion audit. Notice was uncontested; defect, causation, damages, venue and choice of law remained undecided. The jurisdictional result applied to World-Wide and Seaway only. The record showed no direct revenue from Oklahoma service centers, not ownership or control of those centers by the petitioners.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Robinsons buy a car in New York and later travel west
sections.cue: Which businesses sold the car, and who created its Oklahoma connection?
paragraphs: In 1976 Harry and Kay Robinson, then living in New York, bought a new Audi from Seaway Volkswagen in Massena, New York. Seaway was incorporated and operated there. World-Wide Volkswagen, also incorporated with its business office in New York, distributed Volkswagen and Audi vehicles, parts and accessories to dealers in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut under contract with Volkswagen.

The record treated Seaway and World-Wide as independent corporations whose relationships with one another and with Audi and Volkswagen were contractual only. Their sales, shipments, agents, advertising and services served their northeastern territory. Neither closed an Oklahoma sale nor performed an Oklahoma service.

In 1977 the Robinsons left New York to establish a home in Arizona. As Kay drove through Oklahoma, another driver struck the Audi from behind. The impact ruptured the gasoline tank, causing fire in the passenger compartment and severe burns to Kay and two children. The other driver was not part of the Supreme Court litigation. The Robinson Audi was the only World-Wide or Seaway vehicle shown by this record to have entered Oklahoma.

sections.title: The family sues the distribution chain, and two defendants object
sections.cue: Why were the jurisdictional challenges preserved despite other litigation activity?
paragraphs: The Robinsons brought a manufacturers’ products-liability action in the District Court for Creek County, Oklahoma. They alleged that defective design and placement of the gasoline tank and fuel system caused the fire and burns. They named Audi, the German manufacturer; Volkswagen of America, the importer; World-Wide, the regional distributor; and Seaway, the dealer. Harry sued individually and as next friend for the children, while Kay pursued her own injury claim.

World-Wide and Seaway made special appearances contesting personal jurisdiction and submitted evidence of their businesses’ geographic limits. The trial court rejected their due-process objection and later denied reconsideration, leaving the tort suit pending. The companies’ papers also mentioned venue of the subject matter, and they took depositions touching the merits. The Robinsons later claimed waiver, but the trial court classified the appearances as special and Oklahoma’s Supreme Court addressed jurisdiction. The U.S. Supreme Court accordingly treated the objection as preserved.
Volkswagen of America also specially appeared in the trial court, but stopped its challenge there. Its jurisdictional position therefore did not reach the Supreme Court with the two petitioners.

sources.pinpoint: Procedural History: underlying action, special appearances, trial ruling; 444 U.S. 288 & nn.1–4, 289, 295 n.10

sections.title: Oklahoma’s Supreme Court denies immediate prohibition
sections.cue: How did the state court connect these sales to its long-arm statute?
paragraphs: World-Wide and Seaway began a separate original proceeding in the Oklahoma Supreme Court. They requested prohibition ordering Judge Charles Woodson to stop exercising personal jurisdiction over them before the products-liability trial. Woodson’s name appears because that supervisory writ would direct the judge’s exercise of power.

On October 10, 1978, the Oklahoma Supreme Court assumed original jurisdiction but denied the writ. Five justices joined the opinion, two concurred in the result, and one concurred in part and dissented in part. The court analyzed Oklahoma’s long-arm statute. Section 1701.03(a)(3), concerning an in-state act causing tortious injury, did not suffice because the alleged design and distribution acts occurred elsewhere. Section 1701.03(a)(4) reached out-of-state acts causing local injury where the defendant regularly did business, engaged in persistent conduct, or derived substantial revenue from goods used or consumed locally.

The state court inferred substantial Oklahoma-derived revenue from cars’ price and mobility. Because Oklahoma construed its statute to reach federal constitutional limits, statutory and due-process analysis converged. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari from the completed writ proceeding to resolve disagreement among state high courts about remote vehicle sellers. The underlying tort action remained pending; this was review of adjudicatory power, not a products-liability judgment.

sources.pinpoint: Procedural History: original writ and Supreme Court review; 444 U.S. 290–291 & nn.7–9; 1978 OK 131 paragraphs 2–3, 7–20

sections.title: The Supreme Court requires a connection created by each defendant
sections.cue: Why did Oklahoma’s interests not by themselves establish authority?
paragraphs: Justice White wrote for Chief Justice Burger and Justices Stewart, Powell, Rehnquist and Stevens. The Fourteenth Amendment limits a state court’s power to bind a nonresident. Pennoyer expressed that limit through territorial authority; International Shoe framed corporate jurisdiction through minimum contacts consistent with fair play and substantial justice. The majority located the necessary affiliation in the particular defendant’s own forum-directed conduct.

Minimum contacts both protect individuals from burdensome distant litigation and allocate authority among coequal states. Thus convenience and regulatory interest do not themselves supply power over a defendant lacking the required connection. Once that affiliation exists, courts weigh the defendant’s burden, the forum’s interest, the plaintiff’s interest in convenient effective relief, efficient interstate resolution, and shared substantive policies. Oklahoma’s accident, evidence, witnesses, highway-safety interests and convenience concerns could inform reasonableness, but could not replace contacts.

Under Hanson, purposeful availment supplies an act connecting the defendant with the forum’s benefits and protections. The relevant foreseeability is whether the defendant’s own conduct gives reasonable notice of possible suit there. That notice permits insurance, cost allocation, distribution changes or withdrawal from the market. A car’s physical mobility predicts travel; it does not alone predict every state’s authority over the seller.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning: constitutional source, two functions, fairness interests, purposeful availment; 444 U.S. 291–298

sections.title: The majority distinguishes market distribution from the buyers’ journey
sections.cue: What kind of product movement could support jurisdiction, and why was it absent here?
paragraphs: A manufacturer or distributor may establish contacts by placing goods in a distribution stream expecting consumers in the forum to buy them. Deliberate efforts to serve that market give notice of litigation when products cause injury there. World-Wide chose a three-state territory and Seaway operated a New York dealership. Neither made direct or indirect efforts to serve Oklahoma’s market on this record. The Robinsons’ movement after a completed local sale supplied the link.

Oklahoma’s substantial-revenue theory was too attenuated. Expensive cars might eventually travel through Oklahoma, but petitioners’ revenue arose from northeastern transactions, while the customers caused the later local use. The Robinsons also invoked the nationwide Volkswagen service network. The majority stated that petitioners earned no direct revenue from Oklahoma service centers; any marginal commercial benefit from their vehicles’ ability to operate there was insufficient. The record did not establish that these petitioners owned or controlled the centers.

Hess v. Pawloski involved a nonresident’s own use of forum roads, coupled with statutory appointment of a service official for claims arising from that driving. Here the Robinsons, not the commercial defendants, drove on Oklahoma roads. The Court therefore applied ordinary chattel principles rather than creating a special jurisdiction rule for automobiles.

On January 21, 1980, the Court reversed the Oklahoma Supreme Court six to three. Oklahoma lacked personal jurisdiction over World-Wide and Seaway on this record. Audi and Volkswagen of America remained defendants. Adequacy of notice was uncontested, and the Court decided neither defect, causation, damages, venue, governing law nor those other defendants’ liabilities.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning: application, stream, revenue, Hess; Scope; Holding; 444 U.S. 295–299 & nn.11–12

sections.title: Three dissenting writings stress different aspects of fairness and automobile commerce
sections.cue: Why did the dissenters find the Oklahoma forum permissible?
paragraphs: Justice Brennan’s dissent addressed this case and the companion Rush v. Savchuk. For the Robinson litigation he emphasized the Oklahoma accident, hospitalized plaintiffs, local witnesses and evidence, highway-safety interests, and the practical effect of modern transportation and insurance. Minimum contacts should implement fairness flexibly, he argued, with strong forum interests reducing the quantity of defendant contact required.

Justice Marshall, joined by Justice Blackmun, regarded the dealer and regional distributor as deliberate participants in a nationwide marketing and service network. Long-distance travel and authorized service added to a car’s economic value. Selling a mobile product for intended interstate use while benefiting from that network, in their view, supplied purposeful commercial activity sufficiently connected to the place of injury.

Justice Blackmun separately emphasized the automobile’s long-distance function. State roads, police, accident investigation and victim assistance supported both the vehicle market and defense of resulting claims. He would permit the Oklahoma suit against these professional distribution participants.

Those positions remained dissents. The assigned excerpt abridges Brennan and omits Marshall and Blackmun, but the complete source brief preserves all three. The historical majority rule requires separating each participant’s own market conduct from a consumer’s post-sale transport, then assessing fairness once the necessary affiliation exists.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning: Brennan, Marshall and Blackmun; Source verification; 444 U.S. 299–319
